units.translation: 5 L after ἑαυτῶν adds the words τῆς μητρός, which seem to have been once written as a gloss to explain the words τῆς μάμμης (cf. W 53). Luetke rightly omitted these in Pherecydea, Diss. Gott. 1893, 74, since Wil. (in Luetke) preferred to restore Ἱππ. τῆς Μήστορος, Jacoby τῆς 〈Πτερελάου〉 μητρὸς Ἱππ.

to torture her father, wishing to marry Pelops. 〈...〉 having fitted the linchpin of wax, so that when it was crushed in the race, Pelops might win and take her in marriage. But Pherecydes in the eighth book (3 fg 37 a J.) says that he did not put the linchpin in the axle, and thus when the wheel rolled off, Oenomaus fell out. The mares of Oenomaus were Psylla and Harpinna. Myrtilus was the son of Hermes by one of the daughters of Danaus, Phaethusa, or according to others by Clymene, or by Myrto, one of the Amazons.

20 Et. Gen. (A² B) Ἐλέρα: I 761—62. Pherecydes says (Φ. φ. omitted in A), that Elara was the daughter of Orchomenus (ἦν omitted in A), with whom Zeus had intercourse, and he hid her (rather ὤθησεν) under the earth fearing Hera's jealousy, and from the earth Tityos was brought forth; therefore he is called earth-born. (since a space is left in A, B here has λείπει.) And otherwise. Elara, having conceived Tityos by Poseidon, and not being able to bear him in her womb
he relates (λ 576):
